description: We are a multidisciplinary team of 6 passionate members bridging Computer Science and Business at the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Driven by curiosity and a commitment to continuous learning, we combine tech-driven innovation with strategic vision to explore the boundaries of space data and create impactful, real-world solutions.
summary:
**RoverQuest: Beyond the Silent Machines** is an educational 3D space exploration game that takes players on an immersive storytelling adventure across Mars and the Moon, uncovering the stories of historic NASA robotic missions.

Players take the role of an astronaut stranded on Mars or the Moon after their spacecraft crash-lands. To find their way home, they must explore abandoned mission sites, discover historic NASA machines, and uncover the stories behind their missions, technologies, challenges, and scientific discoveries.

Each encounter combines engaging storytelling with interactive learning experiences, allowing players to explore scientific concepts through interactive 3D holograms, physics-based mini-games, and evidence analysis. Rather than simply reading about space exploration, players become part of the story, actively experiencing how these missions contributed to our understanding of the Solar System.

The experience adapts its educational content to different age groups and features TARS, a robotic companion that guides players throughout their journey.

By combining storytelling, immersive exploration, and hands-on learning, RoverQuest transforms the legacy of NASA's space missions into an engaging adventure that inspires curiosity, scientific thinking, and a passion for STEM.

### What it does

RoverQuest is a story-driven educational game about the spacecraft that space agencies have retired, lost contact with or left behind.

1. **Crash-land.** The player enters their name and age. TARS, a robot partner, adapts its wording to the player's age (10–18) and uses their name throughout.

2. **Explore in 3D.** Two complete 3D worlds can be explored with keyboard, mouse or touch, using a radar and a place picker.

   

- **Mars (9 places, restore any 5).** Sojourner, Spirit & Opportunity, Viking 1 & 2, Phoenix & InSight and Ingenuity stand on the plain as 3D models. Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 & 11 and Kepler never went to Mars, so they appear as clearly labelled holo-beacon stations that say where the real spacecraft is today.

- **The Moon (4 sites, restore any 3).** The Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Surveyor 3 and the Apollo laser retroreflectors, on a grey plain with Earth in the black sky.

3. **Play.** Every place has a hands-on mini-game, 14 in total. In each one the player uses how the real machine worked:

   - Signal-Delay Driver (Sojourner), Dead-Wheel Dig and Blueberry Hunt (Spirit & Opportunity), Scoop & Bake (Viking)

   - Marsquake Catcher (Phoenix & InSight), First Flight (Ingenuity), Orbit Hopper (Dawn)

   - Soft Touch on Eros (NEAR Shoemaker), Slingshot (Pioneer), Transit Hunter (Kepler)

   - Lighten & Lift (Eagle), Walk-back Rule (Lunar Rover), Pinpoint Landing (Surveyor 3), Hit the Mirror (retroreflectors)

4. **Discover.** Winning unlocks the real NASA finding, a NASA photo or a labelled illustration, and links to the mission's NASA page and NSSDCA record. Each discovery separates documented observations, scientific interpretations and teaching simplifications.

5. **Launch home.** Restoring enough places brings the ship's systems online. A final launch check is built from the player's own places, and a personalized ending lets the player present what they learned.

### How it works

- It is a static web app (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) with no server-side code, no accounts and no tracking. Progress is saved only in the browser's local storage.

- The 3D worlds use Three.js r128, bundled locally. Terrain, machines, holograms, the astronaut and TARS are built procedurally in code. One shared engine re-skins itself for Mars or the Moon from a per-world configuration.

- 32 NASA/JPL photographs are bundled locally with credits, so the whole game works offline after it is downloaded once. The only exception is an optional NASA video, which loads only when the player clicks it. That makes it useful in classrooms with weak internet.

- The mini-games are self-contained canvas and DOM simulations. Physics are simplified and labelled as such.

- The game is responsive: on phones it shows on-screen movement and interact buttons, larger touch targets and a layout that fits.

- Quality: `node tools/check.mjs` runs 27 automated groups covering code syntax, local links, the image manifest and credits, the science rules of each investigation, the world and place setup, offline assets, save-data validation and the companion's visibility. All 27 pass. The project also includes a Playwright end-to-end and accessibility (axe-core) test suite, and a science fact-check document that maps each claim to a NASA source.

### Benefits

- Learners explore 13 real missions by doing, not just reading.

- It builds scientific thinking: observation vs. interpretation, and real photos vs. models.

- Choice (any 5 of 9, any 3 of 4) gives agency and replay value.

- It is free, runs offline on almost any device and needs no installation or sign-up.

### Goals and intended impact

We want students to see retired spacecraft as a living source of science rather than space junk, and to remember why each machine mattered. Next, we plan to add Arabic and other languages, a teacher mode with class progress, more silent machines, and pilot sessions with students in Egyptian schools.
